newsitem.title: USA: American, pilots in talks with strike hours away.
newsitem.headline: American, pilots in talks with strike hours away.

text.p: American Airlines and its pilots union were locked in intensive negotiations on Friday through a mediator, with little progress reported and a strike deadline just hours away.
As air travelers around the country prepared for the chaos of a strike on the Presidents Day holiday weekend, neither side had much good news after negotiating through the night.
"There's no agreement at this point," said Tim Smith, a spokesman for American, a unit of AMR Corp..

But, Smith said on the ABC programme "Good Morning America," "I think the important fact at this stage is that both parties are still working hard, going back and forth with a mediator between us -- shuttle diplomacy, if you will."
Union spokesman Dave Bates said the two sides were not meeting face-to-face but were negotiating through the government mediator. The union represents American's 9,000 pilots.
The Airline Pilots Union has set a midnight Friday (0500 GMT Saturday) deadline for an agreement to avert a strike that would shut down the nation's No. 2 airline.
The pilots' union on Thursday presented a compromise offer on costs, assuring the carrier that its expenses would be competitive with other big airlines.
Pay for flying the big jets and for flying the smaller jets American wants to buy for its commuter carrier, American Eagle, are key sticking points in reaching a new contract.
American has said it needs to fly the new, small jets with lower-paid pilots if is to compete with other major carriers offering low-cost commuter servives.
Meanwhile, Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, a Republican from Texas -- home of American headquarters in Fort Worth-Dallas -- urged President Clinton to step in to avert the strike.

She said on CNN: "I've urged him to look at the powers he has and to see what the impact is on our area of the country and several other areas of the country and be ready to kick in, if something doesn't happen today."

Clinton has been keeping close watch on the negotiations, the White House said. A report sent to him by the Transportation Department on Thursday said a strike would cost the economy up to $200 million a day.
He could set up a special emergency board to forge a compromise agreement, an action that would prevent a strike for 60 days while the compromise was being drawn up and considered by the two sides.
A shutdown would disrupt travel plans for the 200,000 passengers American flies on its 2,200 routes worldwide every day. It also would play havoc with mail and cargo shipments.

A federal mediator refereeing the talks at a downtown Washington hotel informed the pilots that American had rejected a key union contract proposal covering who should pilot -- and at what pay -- the carrier's smaller American Eagle planes.

Mediators are shuttling back and forth between the two sides offering hypothetical "what if" proposals on a variety of issues in an effort the bring the two sides closer together and prevent a strike.
"We will continue to negotiate for as long as it takes. But (Friday) night at midnight the pilots will be on strike," union spokesman Bates said.
Going into the talks on Thursday evening, Kenneth Hipp, chairman of the National Mediation Board, said he was hopeful an agreement could be worked out in time to avert a strike.

The union had proposed that its pilots fly the American Eagle flights, but with lower pay than pilots flying the regular American aircraft. American, however, wants to continue using lower-paid commuter pilots from a different union to fly the smaller planes.
While the mediator has informed the union of the airline's rejection of the proposal on small planes, union officials said the company itself has not notified them directly.
The dispute also centres around the pilots' pay. They now earn an average of about $120,000 a year.

The union earlier had said it would offer a new pay proposal -- probably less than the 11.5 percent over four years it had sought. The latest reported offer from American was a 6 percent boost over four years.
A strike would ground 2,200 American flights on Saturday and affect about 200,000 passengers. American accounts for about 20 percent of the nation's airline capacity.
The airline is trying to rebook passengers on other carriers and has already cancelled nearly all international flights scheduled for Friday night.

American Airlines spokesman John Hotard said on Thursday the carrier was cancelling 12 of its domestic flights scheduled for Friday. "There are some small domestic airports where we have no permanent place to park the planes if there is a strike, so we decided to cancel those 12 flights."
AMR's stock was off 75 cents at $82.375 in early trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
